utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the Chamber move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Ms. West, good morning. Could you call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prosecution calls Dusan Janc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Janc.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your current job?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I'm an investigator with the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight in Nairobi.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you began your professional career?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I joined the Slovenian police forces in 1993, immediately when I completed my secondary education, as a regular police officer at a police station. After one year I became a criminal investigator, so in 1994, and since then I have been investigating different type of crimes throughout my career. In 2000 I was promoted within the same area. I started working as part of the organised crime unit at the police directorate Kranj in Slovenia. Then between 2003 and 2004, that was June to June, I was sent -- actually seconded as member of the Slovenian police to European Union Police Mission to Bosnia-Herzegovina where I was assigned to Banja Luka, working as an advisor to criminal investigation department to the Republika Srpska. So this was mission monitoring, advising commission to the local business.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was for one year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. That was for one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: After that year, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: In June 2004, I returned back to my Slovenian police force. I again joined the -- I actually returned back to the same Department of Organised Crime Unit. And in June 2006 I joined the ICTY as investigator with the OTP. I left this office in August last year. And I joined the Office of Internal Oversight, or OIOS office, in Nairobi.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So during the period of time that you worked for the OTP, and that's 2006 to 2011, during that time did you prepare reports for the Srebrenica cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout my time spent for the Prosecution being as an investigate for the Prosecution, I have been attached to Srebrenica investigation team. And as part of my duties, I also prepared several reports in relation to -- to Srebrenica investigation of the mass graves and identifications of the people who went missing after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was that first report in March of 2009 for the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. That was my first report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when was your second?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Then I drafted a short corrigendum, I think, month later to that report. In August 2009, I prepared addendum to my report for Perisic trial. In 2010, I prepared another report for Tolimir trial, and I testified in Popovic and Tolimir trial. And now this is the -- the recent one, the latest one, which I put together in December/January this year. Actually, December last year, January this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You noted earlier that the reports were related to the Srebrenica investigation of the mass graves and identifications of the people who went missing. The most current report that you authored for this case, is that the same subject matter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23584, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, you're going to see a -- the screen in front of you, will, in a moment, show a document. Sir, do you recognise this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is a report I prepared for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about the objectives of the report. Can you tell us what those were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: They were four objectives of this report. First, to update my previous reports, in relation to the current number of individuals identified as being Srebrenica victims. The second objective was to present which are the new sites, grave-sites, exhumed in the meantime in Bosnia. The third objective of this report was, of course, to update and also to present findings on surface remains. The people who were found or human remains which were found on the surface over these years. And the last section of my report, that was the fourth objective, would be to present to the Trial Chamber the different DNA connections which I found inside the sources which I used to prepare this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what were your main sources for the report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: My main source to put together all these numbers was the ICMP list of match reports which provided to the OTP in December 2010. That's the list which I used to put together those numbers. Apart from that, I also relied on different documents which were provided to the OTP or I obtained from BiH authorities, and also documentary, some documentary evidence from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. You noted that the first objective of your report was to present the current number of individuals identified as being Srebrenica victims. Can you tell us how it is that that number needs to be updated. Why does that number change?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The exhumation process in Bosnia has not been completed yet, in relation to -- to Srebrenica victims. So they are constantly identifying or locating new graves which are related to Srebrenica victims. And, consequently, the BiH authorities is now in charge to exhume them, to conduct exhumations of those graves. And, of course, when they exhumed them, certain bodies, body parts are found within these graves which need to be identified. And the identification process, the DNA identification process is done by the ICMP, and this has been going on, actually, on -- since 2001, when the ICMP commenced its work. And since then, whenever we get new updated version of the ICMP data, we will get additional numbers or additional individuals found as being identified in the meantime. And that's why my report needed to be updated that reflects the current number of identified individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you noted here that they are constantly identifying or locating new graves which are related to Srebrenica victims. In your most recent report, did you identify any new graves that have been found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. There are two new sites, two new mass graves, in addition to my previous report, which is the last -- which is, actually, 2010 report prepared for Tolimir trial, and those two sites are Bisina cave and Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, before 2001, what entity was responsible for doing exhumations in the region?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Before 2001, the exhumations were done by the ICTY in the region. At that time, the exhumation process by the ICTY stopped and everything was handed over to the BiH authorities. And since then, since 2001 onwards, the BiH authorities have been involved and have been conducting these exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And are those authorities, are they now known as the Bosnian Institute of Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. At that time, it was BiH Federal Commission on Missing Persons which renamed sometime, I think in 2009 or 2008, to BiH Institute on Missing Persons. And they have been involved in these exhumations, I can confirm that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know who Amor Masovic is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Amor Masovic has been the head of this commission and now institute throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we're going to talk about your report itself. And the first question I want to ask you is: How is it that your report is divided? Tell us about the different parts of your report.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: First, you will find six pages of a kind of summary of my report, where I put together different numbers, tables, and we will go over it in a short while. Then to that summary, or to that report, four annexes are attached; Annex A, Annex B, Annex C, and Confidential Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So we've got the beginning, which is the report itself. You noted it was six pages. Now tell us generally what's in Annex A?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: In Annex A, you will find all the -- the graves, mass graves, individual graves, smaller graves which were so far identified and exhumed in relation to the fall of Srebrenica. In addition you will find the numbers of identified individuals which were found in these graves. Also, I think last part will show you some -- some numbers which I put together based on DNA connections, and we'll discuss that later. I think these are the main topics of my Annex A.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how about Annex B, what does that regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It regards surface remains. You will find in the section I'm talking about the surface remains findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What's in Annex C?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Annex C is strictly focussing on DNA connections between the graves, between the primary and secondary graves, or secondary, secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, lastly, what's Annex D?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, the Annex D is a confidential one. It's -- because it's actually the list of people, individuals, with the names, which are identified so far. So whatever I say, for example, in Annex D -- oh, in Annex A, sorry. When I list how many individuals have been identified for a certain mass grave, you will find the actual names in confidential Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go through all these sections in detail, but let's start at the very beginning. We'll start with your report. On the screen you see page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to page 2, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, what we are looking at is 65 ter 23584.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we were informed there are two other corrected versions to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the corrections - and I'll go over those - are only typos that I want to put on the record. But we can look at 23584 and that will be enough for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're looking at page 2. And in the middle, in bold, it says: "Srebrenica victims identified via DNA and other methods in graves." And then the number is 5977. Can you please tell us about that number and what it represents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This number represents, if you follow the text underneath this number, the 5.942 individuals which were so far identified via DNA by the ICMP. On top of it, we have 35 individuals, as you can see down there here, which were identified before the ICMP commenced its work, so some of those individuals were identified between 1995 and 2001, and those were not re-identified by the ICMP via DNA for various reasons, and I found this number of 35 individuals in Dean Manning report. And I included all those names together. You will find who they are in Confidential Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's backup for a moment. You just mentioned Dean Manning. Who's Dean Manning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Dean Manning is a former investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor within the ICTY. He left, if I'm not wrong, 2004, or sometime 2005, the Tribunal. And he has been dealing with exhumations. He did prepare several reports in relation to these exhumations, and my first report was basically updating his findings from before. And as you can see the first paragraph on top of the screen, you know, that also this report which I prepared for this trial should be read in conjunction with his previous reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back to the number. We have the total number or the bolded number is 5977. And then you mentioned that the ICMP had identified at least 5942, that number of individuals. Why is that number not the same as 5977? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: 5977 is -- includes both, 5942 plus 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And these 35 identified individuals you spoke about, you mentioned that they were identified before ICMP got involved. How is it that they were identified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: They were identified, as I was able to -- to find out, through different anthropological methods. And, as I put it here, this is based on ante- and post-mortem data collected by Physicians for Human Rights and International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC. So they were identified by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now we also see another number here, and you say that this number, meaning 5977 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way. Do you see 5977 in -- on this page in bold? You referred to that number several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In bold: "Srebrenica victims identified via DNA and other methods in graves" and then to the right, 5977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah-ha, yes. I see. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now we have another number that I want to talk about and it's in the paragraph below, and it says that: "This number also includes 260 unique Srebrenica-related DNA profiles which have not yet been matched to a missing person." Can you tell us about that number?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I included 260, those unique Srebrenica-related DNA profiles, which, as it says here, have not been yet matched to any missing person. When -- and this was provided to the OTP upon our request by the ICMP. Actually what those represent, these are individuals which have in not been yet matched to any missing person, but DNA profile have been identified. So we have a unique DNA profile, but the -- the ICMP is unable to match this profile to any of the relatives, to any blood donors, so we actually don't know who that person is. We don't have a name. Why I included them into my report is simply because they are all coming out or human remain remains from those individuals were found in mass graves which we know are related to mass executions, and that's why I included those into my report as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we go to next page in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, Ms. West, did you lead Mr. Dean Manning when he was here testifying?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we see the Dean Manning report that is referred to at footnote 4 here. So I -- I'd like to see how those 44 were identified in Dean Manning report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We will have to pull up the ERN number, Your Honour. I think, as you will remember, Mr. Manning had several reports that he talked about. A number of them, I think at least three, regarded issues that do not regard this subject matter. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So -- take your time, so when you are prepared, show us that page and then ... because he specifically referred to that, I'd like to see that while he is here. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If we could go to page 3 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is the third page of your report. And here we see a chart and I want to go over the headings. The first heading we have: "Mass and other graves." Can you tell us about that, what that entails?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: These are mass and, as you can see, other graves, and by other graves, I mean smaller graves and individual graves which -- which are found so far in relation to the fall of Srebrenica. And these are actually the locations where those mass graves were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we go down that list, vertically down, we see Cerska, Nova Kasaba 96, Nova Kasaba 99. Some of these graves are bolded and some of them are not. Can you tell us what that delineates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The bolded ones were exhumed by the ICTY. The others were exhumed by the BiH authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the next column is entitled: "Site code." What is a site code?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Every grave or every site when they were exhumed or even surface remains when collected on the ground is assigned a certain code before the exhumation commenced. And usually, as we can see here, it will be three letters or several letters and some numbers. And we can see for each of those mass graves what code has been assigned to -- to certain -- certain mass -- mass grave, or grave, or location.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who assigns the site code?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The site codes are always assigned by the team who does the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look at 1 as an example. If we can go down a little bit and look at Cancari Road number 1, we see under site code it says "CR01," but then in parentheses, we have something that begins with KAM. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You can see several such examples, and on the next page you will see even more of them and they will always be related to non-bolded mass grave-sites. Why? Because initially the ICTY has located many graves, for example, now we are on this page and we are looking at Cancari site, so they located -- the ICTY located 12 different mass graves along the Cancari Road. And they were allocated numbers, starting from 1 up to 12. We can see it here, Cancari Road 1 would be CR01. Later on, those sites were exhumed and we can see for Cancari Road number 1, for example, that one was exhumed in July 2009. At that time, as I already testified, the BiH authorities were conducting exhumations. So -- and this was exhumed by the BiH authorities. At the time they exhumed the grave, they allocated different site code unrelated to what the ICTY designated before and that's what we can see here. The site which was -- this site was allocated the site code KAM14ZVO. So what we can see in parentheses would be the site code which was actually assigned by the exhumation team at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me if I understand correctly. When we see site codes that have two site codes, one in the beginning and one in parentheses, does that mean that the second one was named by the Bosnian exhumation team who exhumed the grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And this would also mean that all the records which we will see or all the individuals which were found in this grave would be assigned this code. So I won't find any individual on the ICMP list with a site code CR01 as it was designated by the ICTY, but in order to be consistent because the ICTY is using in indictment their own numbers - for example, Cancari Road 1 to Cancari Road 12 - I wanted to present that Cancari Road 1, for example, in order to find out how many individuals is found in this grave, you have to look for specific site code which was assigned by the team who did the exhumation and that one is KAM14 Zvornik, ZVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to the next column from the top, it says: "Exhumation date." I think that is self-explanatory, but why don't you just tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. This is just when this certain mass grave was exhumed, the date or the range.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next column: "Identified individuals." Under that we have the first, which is April 2010, and then the second column, December 2010. Tell us about those columns?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: These are the two columns and what I wanted to present here is to show how the number -- number -- numbers grow during the time. So what we can see under April 2010 column, these are the numbers or the identified individuals included in my previous report. Let's put it in the report prepared for Tolimir trial. Then we have December 2010, so this data I used for -- in order to prepare this report, so you will find the numbers, how many individuals is identified or can be found on the ICMP list as being identified from these sites at that point in time. So it's just that you can compare how the numbers would be growing over the -- over the years, over the period, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are there occasions where the numbers don't, in fact, grow but actually get smaller? An example of that, let's look at Cancari Road 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you, and 9 as well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. You would also find such instances where number would be lower. When you compare both ICMP list, you will find less people on one, whereas more on the other. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can -- we'll talk about more about this later. But just in a general way, tell us how that might happen.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Because ICMP identifies their mistakes, errors. Mostly -- most of those are related, if not all of them, to their errors. For example, they would -- they would have in their -- in their list in April 2010 that a certain individual was found in Cancari 9 grave. Later on they would find out that it was not number 9 but number 8, so it means they would change to number 8 and it means consequently the number in their next list -- next list would fall. And that's -- that's basically the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: So they do identify their mistakes or typos in their data and then they are correcting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to page 5, please, of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is just a continuation of your table but it's the end part of your table, and I want to look at the totals at the bottom. So at the bottom of the table it says: "Srebrenica grave total." And again in the column to the extreme right we see that number that we saw earlier, 5977. Now to the left of that there's a smaller number. Tell us about the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: So the right number, 5977, we already saw before and we discussed about it. And now you can see actually the exact locations where those individuals were found. On the left-hand side, 5765, is the number which was -- which I could find on the previous list. So the number grew for almost -- a little bit more than 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. When you say previous list, you mean the previous Tolimir report; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And below that, we see: "Srebrenica surface remains total." Tell us what those two numbers represent.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It is the same. We can see how the number grew over this period. And this section relates to my Annex B where I'm talking about surface remains. In this we have the number of individuals so far identified as being collected from the surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next row is: "Others." Tell us about this row.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Others are the ones which I separated because either they're not graves or I was not sure what would -- would that be, or I did not have any information on what would those represent. But regardless of all that, they all -- all these individuals can be still found or -- on the ICRC missing list. So they went missing after the fall on Srebrenica, all those 68 individuals. And as can you see, we have Srebrenica -- sorry, Serbia related, so those would relate to the bodies which were found in Drina or Sava river, on the Serbian side, and collected by them after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. Then we have Kozluk surface, where we have, I think, 12 individuals found adjacent to the execution site Kozluk, down almost on the river. So -- and they were found -- when found, they were on the surface. So I was not sure when they were initially placed there were they buried or not. So that's why I'm uncertain, but because they are so close to the execution site, it's difficult to distinguish, are they found on the surface or killed and buried. That's why I put them there. Then we have Godinjske Bare section, this one relates to the execution which took place in Godinjske Bare, and we have a video, the Skorpion video, about this execution. And then with have to uncategorised site, so for those ones I'm not sure what they do present. We asked -- or I asked the BiH authorities to provide us documentation on those individuals and the documentation we received was either insufficient to make -- for me to make any conclusion or we did not receive any documentation on this site. So this that's why I put them there as uncategorised because I was uncertain what we would represent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And when we add those numbers up, at least in the right hand column for the Karadzic case, we get 6747. And is that your total number for victims related to the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. And I put it here, Srebrenica victims in total, which means these are individuals which you can find on the missing list or went missing after the fall of Srebrenica. So -- but we have different -- different cause of death for at least the one found on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll speak more about that shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to e-court page 6, please, the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Janc, why the number for others was reduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was mainly -- the main reason would be this uncategorised site because in the meantime, some of those uncategorised individuals have been not identified but I was able to connect them to certain grave. So they would be found up there. So some of them were taken off the list by the ICMP just because they excluded them as being Srebrenica-related victims so -- and these are the main reasons, because the ICMP took them away from the lists or I was able to connect them to certain site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And 35 individuals identified by Mr. Dean Manning, not through DNA identification, were spread out to individual graves in this chart. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct. And we'll see an example how did I count them and how did I put them separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to page 6 in e-court, which is the final page of just the report section.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, we're now going to start talking about the annex that follows this, which is Annex A, and that regards the number of victims identified, related to the graves. But before we do that, I want to ask you: What was your primary source of information for the results reported in this annex?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: My primary source was definitely the December 2010 ICMP update.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we understand that there's a more recent version of the ICMP update, a January 2012 version. Why did you not use that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. There is a recent -- more recent version, the January 2010 one -- 2012 one, and I haven't used that one because simply I received it too late. I received that version or that data two days before I completed my report. So what I was able to do was only to briefly analyse the data and to extract perhaps the -- the number, or to estimate how many individuals, how many additional individuals would be found on -- on the new list in relation to the list from 2010, which I used for -- to compile my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you came here to The Hague in December and January of 2011, 2012; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. I was here between beginning of December until 15 or 13th of January, in order to put together this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And a few days before you left, is that when the most recent version of the ICMP database arrived?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. Just two days before I finalised my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But, nonetheless, did you do a basic review and analysis of the January 2012 update?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what is the approximate difference between the version you used, December 2010, and the January 2012 version?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Approximate difference would be 80 individuals. So we will find 80 more individuals it identifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should read 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we could move a little bit down on this page to this last paragraph. It says: "Review of the latest ICMP list of DNA matching reports."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is this where you reported the 80, approximately 80, more individuals that you found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. This is my summary of my findings reviewing this latest, January 2012, data.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janc, besides these two versions, so December 2010 and January 2012, have you analysed earlier versions of the yearly ICMP updates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been analysing earlier versions. I would say since 2007 onwards. I believe I reviewed every single version or ICMP update which came in to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is there anything in the December 2010 version, which is the one you used, that was not in keeping with the information that ICMP has normally provided to you over the years?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, they are consistent with their data. So every new version we receive is an update of a previous one. When I say "an update" that would mean, you know, we have new individuals and perhaps we have some corrections made, typos, and that's the key difference between difference versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But was the December 2010 version you used substantially subsumed into the January 2012 version?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm it was substantially subsumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the December 2010 version is 65 ter 23682, and I would tender it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just confused. Could you tell me the reason why -- what's the point of having that 23682 in addition to 23584?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, although it is subsumed into the most recent version, I thought it would be important to have both in evidence in the case that questions would arise. He spoke about very limited differences, but if questions arise as to those limited differences, I think the Trial Chamber should have access to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it would be helpful to highlight them the major differences to understand -- what's the major differences in both. He dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, let's talk again about 2010 versus 2012. Tell us, first of all, you said that there were approximately 80 more individuals in 2012. Besides that, what other differences or what other types of differences are there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah, unfortunately, I didn't have time to analyse them in detail. What I did -- did do was that I went over the lists yesterday, so -- but, again, it's not a detailed analysis because I wasn't having enough time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. West. 23682 is an ICMP match report?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think it's -- excuse me, Mr. President. It should be an ICMP match report from December 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2010. And January report was produced by Mr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4768, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 23681. And that's the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I'm going to ask you about ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the -- the exhibit previously admitted "prematurely" hasn't been released yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a CD, Your Honour, and so we'll upload a surrogate sheet for it. It's quite large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we should put it under seal, shouldn't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that there's a been a motion filed and it's an open issue, so yes. But for right now, it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I want to talk you to in a general way about the ICMP database. And it's presented to us in the -- in the form of a spreadsheet. How is the spreadsheet tabbed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The recent two, and when I am saying "recent two" it is the one I used for my report and the latest one from January 2012, they both have four different tabs. The first tab relates to victims of Srebrenica. Then is a separate tab for victims related to Zepa. And then we have additional tabs, one where they say "excluded," so which means that people are not related to these events. And then is additional tab saying inconclusively associated. So they're not certain if those are related to -- to these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand there are four tabs. One is Zepa, of which we will not talk about. And one is Srebrenica. In regard to the Srebrenica spreadsheets, how did the ICMP sort the names?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: First, I would just like to emphasise that for my analysis, I used just the Srebrenica tab. I disregarded the other tabs. I have not included any of the other individuals in other tabs. And to answer your question, every spreadsheet, whenever you open it, is sorted by the missing person alphabetically.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 23681. And this is a sample page of which everyone in the courtroom should have a big chart version of this because it's hard to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we can all work off of this because is shouldn't be broadcast anyways. So this is 65 ter 23681 and it's -- would be the first e-court page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, why are we using a sample page from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to make sure that Mr. Karadzic and the Defence has it in front of him. Mr. Karadzic, do you have it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If that's the one, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, we're all looking at a sample page that you put together. Why are we actually using this instead of actually just looking at the ICMP database?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Because it's so many entries you have in this spreadsheet, I think more than 14.000 entries, and in order to print all those out it would be more than 700 pages, so -- and that's why I printed out just the first page or the first, I don't know, perhaps 30 entries which appear on the spreadsheet when you open it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We see two colours in the entries. We have like a grey/blue colour and then a yellow colour. What do the two colours mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: We have two colours, yes, and those on the original spreadsheet would be the grey, only grey and yellow. The grave -- the grey colour is the background colour, I would say, the ICMP background colour, and this is my understanding, of course. And the yellow colour would represent the individuals which were added to this new list, so these are the new individuals added to their list in addition to their last list provided to the OTP. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to go across the top header and talk about these labels, which was done last week in this court as well, but it's important for your testimony. So let's start with the first one which is entitled: "MP." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: MP stands for missing person. Individuals listed down here are the ones identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And several of these names we see in the middle of the name a different first name that is in parentheses. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. In parentheses we have father's name so it would appear on this list as first name -- actually, first is last name of the individual, then father's name, and then it would be first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Then we have date of birth, which is self-explanatory. And the third column is protocol ID. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Protocol ID refers to DNA sample and it is assigned by the ICMP. So every DNA sample would go -- would get one protocol ID. It would refer to one individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we'll speak more about this number when we talk about connections. But let's move on. And the next column is case ID. Tell us what that represents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Apart from protocol ID, the case ID is one of the -- or was one of the most important entries in order to compile my report, and this case ID would refer to the exhumation site. I see from those numbers and letters and numbers, or codes, where this particular body or body part was found. For example if we take a look into the first one, where we have KAM10ZVO, I know that this person was found -- or body part of this person was found within the Cancari Road 10 mass grave. Then we have certain numbers next to it and those relate to the body part. This is labelled during the exhumation which -- where every single body or body part would get a number. So this particular body part was found in a grave and assigned a sequence number, 1380.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's stop for a moment and focus on the methodology that you used to come to the total number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can move to page 2 of this sample sheet. So the next page. Again, this is 65 ter 23681, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be sure, if you read out the last four digits of the ERN.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. And we are looking at the last four digits, 2186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your first step was when you were trying to figure out total number of victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: What I would do first is that I would sort this spreadsheet by case ID and this is now in front of us an example when I sorted it by case ID. Now we can see that missing person, the first column, is not sorted by alphabetically anymore, but we can see that case ID is sorted alphabetically.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why did you do it by case ID?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Because now I'm looking for particular grave-sites or particular site codes and trying to establish which individuals are found -- are located in different grave-sites, and that's why I'm sorting them by case ID, because then I'm extracting every single entry into a separate spreadsheet in order to get spreadsheet related to one mass grave, one grave, one location, whatever. So I go through the entire list, through all those 14.000 entries, and I'm extracting or copying or copying every single entry into separate spreadsheet. So now I have a spreadsheet in front of me which would represent, for example, one grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So if we can back up for a second. When we look at case ID and in this example at the top the first several begin with BIS01SEK. Should we understand that those letters represent a different grave-site or a different place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: So I always look into the first part of the case ID, which in this case is BIS01CEK [sic], and all with the same case ID at the beginning would relate to one grave-site because the number after are, as I already explained, the numbers assigned to different body or body parts during the exhumation. So I would be looking for the first part of this case ID, so this would tell me the site code. Of course, in order to separate and then to find out where those are or what those site codes represent, I need to have a background knowledge or information and, you know, lots of documentation to identify each and every single one. And that's exactly what I have been doing over this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You mentioned at line 18 CEK. Did you mean BIS01SEK?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know offhand what site that refers to? You may not know.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I know all the sites. This is Bisina cave, Bisina 01 cave, and why I take this one as an example, it's just because Bisina -- Bisina grave, actually this is Bisina grave not Bisina cave - I have to correct myself - because Bisina mass grave appears the first one from -- on the list, if you are sorting them alphabetically.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the next page of the sample sheet. And this is the ERN ending in 2187. You mentioned earlier that you sort them by grave-sites and you create separate spreadsheets per grave-site. Is this one of those separate grave sheets?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. This is the one which is created when I separated them from the main data. So I get all the -- all the individuals which were found or body parts which were found within one grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. As to this page, 2187, and the following page, 2188, do these two pages represent the sample for that particular site, Bisina cave? Excuse me, just Bisina.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah. Those all relate based on the case ID. You can see that they all bear the same site code, and those all relate to Bisina grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go back to the previous page, second page, i.e., the page ending with ERN 2186. Do you have it with you, Mr. Janc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You told us that this is a result of your sorting out the database based on case ID and you said this is the first page. Why do we not see all the cases which we see on the separate spreadsheet per grave? All the issues that appear on this first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right and I will correct myself. This is not actually the first page. This is some page after. What I wanted to present here -- and, of course, many entries are before that. This is the first mass grave which actually appear on the ICMP list, if you sort it by case ID. But I didn't want to present on this sample page just -- just Bisina, Bisina cave, or Bisina grave, but I wanted to include, as can you see down there, you have different site codes. I wanted to present to the Trial Chamber, okay, this is when you sort it out you will get different entries. And you can see down there you have Bljeceva, that's what I wanted to present. But actually this is not the first page, no, when you sort it by case ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is this as a result of second sorting-out exercise or the last page of the exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If you are talking about 2186, so let -- let's say, I would sort it by case ID. Then in this case I would go, now, for example, on page number 5, and I would print out this page number 5 just to capture not only the Bisina site but also the other sites which -- which are sorted alphabetically after Bisina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that this is the page where the BIS -- Bisina-Sekovici grave-site appears the last.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct. Because you can see the numbers that are the last one on the list for Bisina site, and then other site would appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we can go back to 2187. I just want to, at this point, continue with the header information. The last header we spoke about was case ID. And then the next column is: ID ICMP. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is again the number assigned by the ICMP and relates to the missing person.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next is: Site name. What is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is the site of exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Site co-ordinates. What is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It would tell us where this was exhumed, what is the exact location of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Explain to us what jurisdiction means.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: So my understanding is that this is institution which submitted the DNA sample to the ICMP for further examination, for DNA examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at least on this page, we see: All BiH/Federation commission in this entire row. What is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It's the same BiH Commission on Missing Person I was talking about before.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this the group that was in charge of the exhumations after 2001, after the ICTY stopped doing it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Next is: Date of submission.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: My understanding is that this is the date when the DNA sample was submitted to the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Date of disappearance.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is the date which is attributed to every single individual by the ICMP. They are not strict as to when certain people went missing, because they simply -- if they related to Srebrenica event, they put usually the date of 11 of July because their mandate is different than the ICMP one. On the ICMP list of missing persons you would get much more reliable results as to when these persons went missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you mean the ICRC missing persons list?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the ICRC information on this particular column would be more reliable?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And that's why I haven't relied on any of this data from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So now we've come to this last column which is entitled: "Type of report." And before we talk about that, I want to make sure that I understand correctly that the first step in your methodology to come to a total number is to separate, first, by site code or location, grave location, and then create separate spreadsheets of those locations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your next step?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Now we have this type of report where you can see entries as being main case or reassociation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us what "main case" means?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Main case is assigned to individual or to -- to DNA -- DNA match or sample which is first related to -- or found first time by the ICMP. So whenever ICMP identifies particular individual for their first time, they would assign this body or body part as a main case. And since we have so many body parts found in these Srebrenica-related graves, primary, secondary graves, usually there are more identification -- identifications done for one individual because we have instances where one individual was found in two or even three different grave-sites. In this case, whenever they subsequently identify additional body part of that same individual, that body part would be labelled here as reassociation to the main case. So one individual will always have only one main case, and it may have no, one, or whatever number you want, reassociations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so is it possible that when we look at the spreadsheet, there could be duplicate listings of the same name in the left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. You will very often find duplicate names in the left-hand column. And also on this spreadsheet, we can see, if you go down to the case where you can see reassociation on the right-hand side, you will see that person appears twice. Once as a main case and other name as a reassociation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Janc, it is impossible for an individual to appear twice as main case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. That's my understanding. There is not a single individual on the ICMP list which would appear twice at being assigned twice as a main case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, when you were counting up the number of individuals associated with the graves, did you ever count reassociations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why not --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: That's what I excluded, of course, not to duplicate the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when you made that count, did you only look at main cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. For example, this spreadsheet we have in front of us, I would further - that would be next step in my methodology - further filter it out by type of report, just in order to get only main cases or extract only main cases from this list, and this would be now the list or the number of individuals found in particular grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we may look at the next page ending in ERN 2188, tell us about this, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is exactly what you get when you filter out the main cases from -- from that last column. And so this would now represent -- this would be now one of -- of the total numbers used in my report because on top of it, I added some additional individuals. We'll go over that soon. But as can you see, they're all now main cases. So we -- I got rid of all the reassociations so not to duplicate any of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to 65 ter 23584, the report, and have page 90 in e-court, please. For the remainder of these exhibits, they're not to be broadcast, please. These are from Annex 12 -- excuse me, Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is -- we're looking now at your results for Cerska; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to page 91 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we have the first page of the Cerska results, starts with the number 1. And this list continues on. And I want to show you the last page of this, which is page 98 in e-court. And here we have names reaching to or -- let's focus on line 138. 138 and below that in numbers, those 138 people, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You can see in total the last number is 149 so this is the total number of individuals so far identified from Cerska grave. And up to -- up to 138, we have individuals listed which I found on the ICMP list. So these are all the main cases which I was able to retrieve from the ICMP list as being related to Cerska. You can see they all bear the same case ID which is -- or the same site code, CSK.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us about 139 through 144. What are those?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. These are six cases out of those 35 which were identified before the ICMP commenced its work. So those are identified through other means and represent the six of those 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's the 35 that we spoke about on page 2 of your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now looking at 144 to 149, what do those represent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From 145.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I want to move now to Annex C, which regards DNA connections between different graves. Can you tell the Chamber why it is that you looked for connections between graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah, we know that all of the biggest mass graves related to Srebrenica event were tampered with at some later point and the bodies removed from the primary location and into the secondary location, secondary mass graves. And doing that, of course, body parts of one individual would be found perhaps in two different locations. And that was very important for my analysis, just to -- to further corroborate the evidence which are already in -- known to the OTP. And the DNA connections is one of the best evidence to prove that certain graves are connected between each other. When I say "connected," it means that bodies or body parts were disposed from one location to another. So following these connections, you will get the pattern or you will get the clear indication and clear evidence of which of those connections are connected between each others. So in that way, that's why I put lots of effort to extract data from the ICMP list to find those connections within the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's talk about the steps you took to do that. What was step number one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. When I opened -- again, you know, I started from beginning. I opened the spreadsheet, and I first sorted it by -- by protocol ID. Because, as I said, the protocol ID is unique. It represents one DNA sample which is linked or matched to particular missing person. So for this kind of analysis, I needed to know the protocol ID numbers and how many of them would appear. For example, the same protocol ID, if it appears several times, it would mean there is a connection. Or at least, say, there are several body parts found of one individual. So then I needed to -- to look into further when I found that there are several parts. It means that there are same protocol IDs, for example, five, I have to take a look into the next column which is case ID, in order to identify, okay, are all these five body parts found in the same grave, or are they found in different locations.

So date of birth is the same. Then protocol ID, it's -- you know, I already say -- said that it's important what the number says. So all the numbers are the same. You know, whenever we have reassociation, R is attached. So now when I see this entry, okay, I know there are five different body parts found, identified, so I'm looking at -- into the case ID where I see that we have two different site codes. For example, in this case, Budak 1 and Zeleni Jadar, it's -- it's written 8 but it refers to Zeleni Jadar 4. So it means two body parts of this individual were found in Budak grave; the other three in Zeleni Jadar 4 grave. It shows something different so just the connections between the graves.

utterances.text: Okay. So should we understand that this means that there are five parts of this body found in two different places?

utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.text: Maybe before I go to this one, I would like to just add on -- on -- on the previous one. Regardless of the fact that we have five pieces of -- or five body parts distributed within two different graves, I would count this as one connection. So between grave one to grave two, regardless of that. So if there three or five or whatever how many body parts in a grave, I would just count it as one connection in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or one case of connection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. One case of connection. So we will go into the area where we have more. I think we're coming to this example right now and I will explain how did I count -- if you have three body parts found in three different graves, how did I count those. I'll explain. And we have example of this individual, the following one, so we see here what happens, and we haven't touched upon this area yet. Very often you will find within the ICMP data the sibling cases. So like here we have last name of the person, then we have father's name, and then we have two first names. So these are sibling cases, so-called, so which means that the ICMP was able to -- to find one DNA sample, but -- and they actually assigned the number to that sample, which means it is related to one person but they were unable to link that sample to one of two brothers, or three, or even -- we have even four brothers. So they were uncertain who of those two brothers was found. We have -- very often what will happen -- for this particular case, I don't know. But you will find, for example, in next entry, again, missing person would be identified as the same as these two ones, but what will be different will be the protocol ID in that other case. So in this case, if I find, like here, sibling case, we have two brothers, and I find then for those two brothers I have two protocol IDs, I'm able to conclude that both were identified. What I am unable to confirm is which of those two was found in which grave. So -- and that's why I'm saying the protocol ID for my DNA connection analysis is the most important part, or most important information which I am seeing in their data. Because if we go left -- or right to the ID ICMP number, you would see that we have two numbers in this case. So because they cannot distinguish between the two brothers and every single person in their data, missing person, has their unique number, but in this case they cannot distinguish who of those two numbers was found there. They can only say, yes, this is one person, based on protocol ID. The DNA sample, you know, is related to one person. So, a background about this protocol ID. And now we can focus on case ID. In this case we see that body parts of this one individual were found in three different graves; Budak 1, Budak 2, and again Zeleni Jadar 4. In this case we have three connections and I would count these particular graves three times in -- as it relates to DNA connections. So because we have connection between grave A and B, we have connection between grave A and C, and we have another connection between grave B and C.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you said -- sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. And then underneath, I put the total number of connections for each cluster of the graves. utterances.text: So that we have that many connections between those two sites. I found that many connections in ICMP data.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And this general theory and methodology, is this repeated for all the sites, all the major sites?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was a little bit more difficult for Kravica or Glogova related primary and secondary graves because it is so many connections. And we may go to those charts and we'll see --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get there. May we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.text: I will make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we go to the next e-court page, which is 84.
