utterances.text: Could Ms. West please move a little closer to the microphone for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the chart that ends in 7278. And here we see two boxes on top. Can you tell us about these graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. It's again a sub-chart of the general one. On the left-hand side we have Orahovac primary grave-site, and then related secondary graves and the connections between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, again, we have the red lines. And is that the connection between the primary grave and the secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And you might have noticed different colours, different boxes, different colours. For example, Orahovac, Lazete 2 and Hodzici Road 3, they both have brown colour, whereas the others are green. So whatever is in brown colour, these are the graves exhumed by the ICTY. The green colours would represent the graves exhumed by the BiH authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when we look over to Petkovci dam and we see the secondary graves, we have four in green and one in brown. And so that one in brown was exhumed by the ICTY; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Dam near Petkovci was exhumed by ICTY and also Liplje 2, secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can move to the next e-court page, which is 85. And in hard copy that is 7279.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This, on top, says Glogova 2, Glogova 1, and Kravica. Tell us what this represents.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is another sub- chart. That one relates to Glogova mass graves and related secondary graves. Because you will see we have so many connections and so many graves related to this site, I first wanted to present you how many connections we have between primary and secondary graves. That's why we only have red lines on this chart. On the far right corner, up corner, you will see Kravica warehouse and it's again in different colour because this is related to execution point. We did find one connection between Kravica warehouse and Zeleni Jadar 2 grave, secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we were to move to the next e-court page, 86, and the next chart, 7280, are these the same locations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Everything -- all locations are still the same on this chart. What is different is that here it is represented -- actually, the secondary graves connections are represented. So how many connections we have between secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is that why we only see blue lines on this page?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Correct. Because the blue represents secondary grave connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, lastly, if we can go to the next page. It's the last page of the handout, 7281, tell us what you did here.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Now, you can see the merged -- those two Glogova-related primary and secondary graves connections merged in one. And you see the network of connections which were established between those graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now all this information that you have put in visual form, did you also put these in table form in your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It's part of Annex C.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 23584; e-court page 48.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we see a table that says: "DNA connection between ..." And then in a second column: "Number of DNA connection cases." Tell us about this table.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the table, and you will find exactly the same connections in those charts. And originally in my report this table is in colour, and they would be the same colours as -- as -- as the one in my chart. So this is in black and white on the screen. But, for example, Orahovac 1, Hodzici 5 would be green and so on and so forth. So each colour would represent something which I described in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So the colour corresponds between your table and the charts themselves.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. It should, although I have to check.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 23584; e-court page 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now that we've looked at the total numbers in each grave-site and the connections from the primary to the secondary and, in some cases, secondary to secondary, I want to look now at how those grave-sites are connected to the execution sites. So on e-court page 40 of your report - if we can go down a bit, please - we have another table. The first column is: "Execution site." Can you tell us what this table represents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's again a breakdown of connections which I found examining the data. This table will tell us how many individuals is so far identified, if you combine primary and secondary graves, actually, if you count both together, and then you link them to the execution site. So we know which execution site is related to primary and secondary graves. And this is very well reflected in the charts which we just presented and it's based on DNA connections.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we're looking at right now regards Kravica. If we can go to the next page, which is page 41, we can see that the Kravica total is 1374. Then we have Orahovac, appears the total is 841. Petkovci, 815. Kozluk, 815. Then Branjevo and that actually goes onto the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on, Kravica said "and others." Kravica and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next page for Branjevo, that's the number of 1735. Mr. Janc, I noticed that at least three of these numbers are in the 800s. One is 815, one is 815, one is 841. Branjevo is 1735, almost the double of 800. Can you tell us what the significance of that is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It was quite significant to me putting all these numbers together to come to a figure of 800 or almost 800, around this number, for every site. Now I'm talking about the sites Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, and Branjevo-Pilica, excluding Kravica, but all those five sites -- and we know that Branjevo-Pilica, they are actually two sites included into this primary grave because they include the individuals killed at Branjevo Military Farm also individuals in Pilica Dom. So and one -- 1700, it would be a little bit more than double a number of 800. And it was a kind of -- you can see from these numbers there was a pattern how many people would be killed at a particular location, and thinking of that, you know, the -- and the only logical explanation for me would be know, you know, okay, this is because that many perhaps transportation means were at the -- their disposal for transporting prisoners to one particular location, and that's my -- my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 01998, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a document. It's dated July 13th, 1995. The 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, and it's to General Gvero from General Tolimir. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the first paragraph -- above the first paragraph it says: "Accommodations of prisoners of war." And it says: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all prisoners of war from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that space with," and there's not a known word," has been arranged for 800 prisoners of war in the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade in Sjemec." Tell us what significance that is for you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You know, it's the number of 800, that one stands out. And when I put together these numbers, I did remember that document, and I linked the two. Because we can see here that 800 is the number most probably which can fit in their transport means at the time. So -- and they were making up space in Sjemec area which is totally different area away from Srebrenica. It's close to Zepa, actually. We did investigation on that site and if any prisoners were brought there, and we didn't find any. So those prisoners were never brought there, so we know for the reason why, because they were -- because you can see actually this is dated 13th of July, when most of them, except for the Kravica ones, are still alive. And, yeah, my conclusion is that those 80 -- 80 prisoners were executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Those 800?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Sorry, 800. And perhaps it not that clear from the original document, the number it can't be seen perfectly, but there is another handwritten version of this same document and you can see the number of 800 there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that version is connected to this English version. If you continue on this document, it says that: "They can be guarded with their own forces and would use them for agricultural work, maintaining the horse, pig, and sheep farm. If you send them to this sector, this must be done at night using Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade transport and troops. It would be best if this is a new group which has not been in contact with the other prisoners of war." So when it talks about the horse, the pig and the sheep farm, do you know anything about that? Did your investigation reveal anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: There was a farm at the time at this place. So that's all we know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4769, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I want to go now to Annex B in your report. It is 23584, e-court page 44, and this regards surface remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before doing this, just I wanted to confirm if my understanding was correct, Mr. Janc. Shall we go back to Annex C. I take it it's on page 48 on the same document. Yes. And shall we show him the next page. And next page. And next page. So here we see total cases in the number of 885. What I'd like to confirm with you is this: The notion of number of cases is separate or different from that of number of individuals identified. Put otherwise, let me give you an example. If one -- if parts of one individual were found in four separate graves, then you can count six cases of connection. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Your Honour, you're perfectly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when we talk about 885 cases of connection, can you tell us how many individuals we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would need to count, but my assessment would be, but pure assessment, around 500, maybe up to 600 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P03975, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, yes, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did find the exact number. It is actually included into my Annex C, where there is an index of all the individuals listed. So if you go further, a few pages further, so you -- we'll get to the actual Annex C index. This one can be broadcast. It's not -- because no names included onto it. And the last entry number is 795. So it means this number, 885, would represent 795 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I think now we can now probably turn to P03975. And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One further question. What did you mean by not counted in the Annex C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So I will need a little bit more time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, we are talking about page ending ERN 7255. And the number 795 appeared on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. We have these 556 cases which I also found on the ICMP data being connection between different sites but I haven't counted them for purposes of my report. There were various reasons for that and most of them relate -- relate to the connection found between Ravnice 1 and Ravnice 2 grave. With Ravnice 1 this is -- actually, these are both primary graves. They haven't been disturbed and they are just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the grave name. Name of the grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Ravnice 1 and 2. Those were designated as two separate graves but they are adjacent to -- next to each other, so -- but they were exhumed at two different occasions. So because it is actually not really clear that these are two graves, I haven't counted them as a connection. And then why I excluded those. Then we have a set of graves which would cover, for example, connections between Glogova 5 and Glogova 7 because this is actually all Glogova 2, bigger Glogova 2 graves, but Glogova 5 and Glogova 7 are sub-graves within the Glogova 2. I haven't counted those. Then we have sets of cases. For example, Liplje 1 and Liplje surface, where you have connection between body parts found in a grave and body parts found on the surface, discovered on the surface. And this was very obvious or very often that that happened in Liplje because, according to my understanding and what I was able to find out, the Liplje graves, which are related to Petkovci dam, were the most difficult to -- to -- to examine because there were so many body parts in it. There were smashed in so many body parts because of obvious reason of the terrain which is at Petkovci which are -- where there are rocks. Because initially people were buried there and covered with -- with the rocks and everything, and many body parts were -- were smashed. So that's why we have so many little body parts found in Liplje grave, and also later on, so many were collected from the ground in subsequent years. So not everything what was exhumed during exhumation was obviously collected from the -- from the area. So this will show us actually there is a connection between the grave and -- and these bones found on surface. Then we have, I think, several of them which I didn't count because they were illogical to me. Illogical because they are connected -- for example, if we take a look into the first one, there is a connection between Cerska and Hodzici 2, Hodzici 3 road. We know that Cerska is a primary undisturbed grave and it will be very unlikely that there is any connection established between those two sites. Connection between Hodzici 2 and Hodzici 3 is most probably a correct one but not back to the Cerska 2. What happened in this particular case, I know we are talking about twins and most probably the DNA or the ICMP was unable, of course, because you cannot distinguish between the twins with DNA examination. So that's why they actually count one person, but I would say these are actually two individuals. Both brothers are found, one in Cerska, one in Hodzici. But still for my purposes I counted only one because they are assigned one main case. So that's why I excluded this one as being a connection. But then we have also connections like entry number 7 between Glogova 5, which is primary grave, and Kozluk 3 and Cancari 3. I would say Kozluk 3, Cancari 3, yes, connection. Glogova 5, Kozluk 3, it's again illogical. Why that happened, I don't know. It would need further clarification. I think I sent question to the -- to the ICMP. They clarified that in a way that there might be labelling mistake. For example, it might happen in the future that, for example, Glogova 5 grave or Glogova 5 site code will be -- will be replaced with something -- with someone -- with something else, saying, oh, there was a typo error. So that's why I excluded, you know, these particular cases as well. Because they are so far away and, you know, especially if you have connection between Glogova site and any of the northern secondary graves, there must be, according to my understanding, something wrong with the actual identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I want -- meant to tell you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. And these were basically the reasons why I excluded these individuals, in total 56 of them, but I presented them in my table in order to show everybody what I can find in ICMP data, what I was able to extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. P03975.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're now going to talk about surface remains. Can you define that for us. Tell us what surface remains means.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Surface remains are body parts or bodies which were left behind, never buried, and when -- and found on the surface. Over the years, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the course of your investigation and your report writing, did you receive information that surface remains were found in the area of the former Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And from where did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: First, this was -- my first source when I started putting together my initial report, the source was Dean Manning's report because he included surface remains into his report. But he wasn't specific. He didn't list how many individuals, but he just listed some sites where those surface remains were collected over the years. And, of course, I inquired further to get more reliable data on those surface remains. I approached the Bosnian Institute or then Commission on Missing Persons and they provided us a table with all the surface remains cases collected from the ground around Srebrenica towards Baljkovica, so in this area, in Podrinje area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to stop to show you the report, but the sources from which you received that information, that's listed in Annex B; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. All my sources are there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And we're now looking at a map. And this -- is this a map that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what do the lines represent?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is the route, the line, the red line represents the route which the column -- the route of the -- the column towards free territory, from Srebrenica up to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 4779. And if we can have page 14.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Is that part of an exhibit, this map? Because we will need it in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was Exhibit P3975. It was in map 5 -- number 5 in the map book.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 14 of 65 ter 4779.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This is the map created by the same commission, Bosnian Commission on Missing Persons, upon our request and this was based upon the data which provided to me, to us, regarding surface remains. So -- and the map would show us the distribution of those surface remains within the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we see a bunch of circles and this is in the area of Srebrenica. Tell us what the circles mean.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: The circles would mean where the surface remains were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, page 15. It's a closer version of the same map. This is just closer up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On this, we see right in the middle one area that has many circles. What is the name of that area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Let's put it Pobudje area. That's how I also named it in my report. And we can see the big cluster of dots there, so the distribution of surface remains is the highest in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if go north of there, we see another small area that has a high concentration. What is that area called?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. So now we are referring to the cluster under Zvornik, let's say, west to Zvornik. This area I designated as Snagovo area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then going even further north of that, we have another cluster. What is that area called?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: That area north of Zvornik is called Baljkovica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go to the next e-court page which is an even closer version of this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We see that it is concentrated on one area. What is this area again?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This area is called Pobudje area. And then we see some other dots around which are north of Srebrenica or west. Those surface remains would be designated in my report as other -- other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In total for your investigation, how many surface remains did you count that were associated with the events of Srebrenica in July?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And will we see that number in your Annex B?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I won't go there just now. But I want to give you an example of surface remains that recently came up in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to Sanction, please, and if we can also go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not tendering that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, I am tendering it. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted -- I mean 65 ter 4779.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4770, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to look into the cases of those six people that I read off? Specifically in regard to where their remains were found.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I checked those names against the ICMP list.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I have to consult my notes, but I found --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You don't have to read the names off but maybe you can give us the initials.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. That four of those individuals listed were found on the surface and two of them in graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What grave? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me be specific. Those four which were named by -- by the witness as being killed at that spot, were found all in Pobudje area, so still on the surface. One of them in Liplje 4; and one of them is either in Hodzici 1 or Lazete 2 because we have the problem with the siblings in this case. So in one of those two locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, would the information that you uncovered support the suggestion that these people were found in a number of mass graves but were killed in combat in a single location?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Those people were not found in any of those mass graves. They were just left behind where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about another individual and this is something that came up just yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P4759, and may it not be broadcast, please. I'm looking at page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I clarify something?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: In relation to -- I check the testimony of Dr. Parsons last week specifically about this topic, only about this topic. I was given his transcript, and the problem I see with -- with him is related to what he referred as being, for example, the site code attributed to mass grave. So he wasn't correct. Because what he said is that, for example, the site code which was put to him, B.KAM.BR, would be related to one of the Kamenica or Cancari graves, because he identified KAM which would stand for Kamenica. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good day, Your Excellencies. Good day to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you for having met the Defence team yesterday, and I hope this will be of assistance to us. I hope it will help me complete my cross-examination in time and in a smooth manner. I'd like to ask you the following. Have I understood this correctly, you went to police academy and completed a course at the police academy; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a secondary police school. After that, I also completed college for police and security studies. After that, post-graduation degree I obtained at the faculty of criminal justice in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did you work for the police? What sort of duties did you perform in the police force prior to becoming an investigator?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I was a, let's say, regular police officer for a year, between July 1993 to September 1994. At that time I became criminal investigator at the police station, so at the lower level. So I was dealing basically with minor criminal offences, like burglaries, thefts, frauds, but also going to the crime scenes of serious crimes, make sure that they are secured, protected, and this kind of criminal activities or investigations. Later on I moved to the organised crime department within the police directorate Kranj where I have been dealing mostly with serious crimes related to organised crime. That was in 2000, where I stayed until 2003, when I was sent for one year to Bosnia-Herzegovina being an advisor to Criminal Investigation Department of Republika Srpska police forces. And then I returned back to my forces in Slovenia in 2004, in June, where I joined the same unit, organised crime department unit. In 2006, I became an investigator at this Tribunal. And since August last year I'm investigator still with the Office of Internal Oversight Services. So, let's say, for the last 18 years I have been involved in criminal investigations, investigating all sorts of crimes, being minor or really serious and big crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would your profession be called in our former system and in our language? Would the title used be inspector? Would that be the name one would give to your profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. You know, it's always up to the system and to the organisation. At one point I was -- my title, official title, was criminal investigator inspector or inspector for criminal investigations or something. It is difficult to translate. But, yeah, they used to call us inspectors. But later on we became investigators. So it changed a lot, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. Could you please explain how and in what order the events unfolded. In fact, am I correct when I say the following: You would receive a criminal report from the regular police force; isn't that correct? And then you would inform the prosecutor of the case or you would launch an investigation yourself before the prosecutor's office initiated such an investigation? How did these things work, in fact, in our former system, or, rather, in your former system?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: So I would be focussing on the system I went through, how it was, and I think it is still organised in the same way. It is whenever you get information or a report about the crime being committed, so -- and this might be various sources. It's not only from police officers. You might come across any such reports or incidents by yourself. So in any such instances you would inform the prosecutor about the crime or possible crime committed and then we would start our investigation independently of the prosecutor, informing the prosecutor what we are doing. So investigation, it's up to the police forces in my country. Now, more these days it's more in corroboration with the prosecutor, but when I was there, it was more up to the police -- police forces investigator to run the investigation. If you want certain measures or -- to be implemented during your investigation, of course, you need to get the permission, for example, from -- from the prosecutor or even we approached the judge, for example, if we wanted to search a house. In that case, the judge would give us an order to search a house or person or this kind of stuff. Or, for example, if you attend the crime scene, so you have to inform judge and the prosecutor. And then they decide if they attend or not. If they say no, then it's up to the investigator to do this crime scene investigation himself. And then when investigation is done, when everything is completed, I would submit my report, my findings, or I would actually submit my, let's say, criminal charge to the prosecutor. Then it's the prosecutor again do decide if -- if there enough evidence to bring this case in front of the court. So that's basically the system in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the role of the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, certain activities should be -- should be ordered by the judge. So we would request these -- or we would submit such requests to the investigative judge. So he is the one, let's say, in the middle. When you are conducting investigation, you would always approach the investigative judge in order to get the search warrant from him. And whenever you would, for example, arrest the suspect, you would bring such suspect along with your report to the investigative judge, and he examined -- examines him first. And then it's up to the prosecutor to decide if they will start the investigation but the judicial investigation. And if this is then started, the investigative judge will run this -- will run this investigation, judicial investigation. Only after that, when this is completed, judicial part of the investigation, everything is brought in front of the court, in front of the judges, when the trial starts, so when the investigation is done by an investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that the investigating judge returns all the investigating material to the prosecutor and only then the decision is made whether to indict or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Before that, and that's what -- why I emphasise that we would submit criminal charge in Slovenia to the prosecutor. This is not indictment yet. Of course, then it's up to the prosecutor to decide about investigation. And when he gets all the information or the results of the investigation done in front of investigative judge back, then it's up to him to decide regarding the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now move onto another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that what you were doing -- in fact, the initial material was expert material from pathologists, exhumation experts, et cetera, processed by Mr. Manning, and that material you then took over to continue updating; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC

utterances.text: So neither by training, nor occupation, nor by assignment did you review the expert material. You just took it for granted as a done deed. Matter closed.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It's not as simple as that. I reviewed that material and also the subsequent material which -- which was submitted to the OTP in subsequent years. And I reviewed that material as well, and, of course, used the findings of these experts to make the conclusions in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of all this initial expert material, what did you critically review and analyse? Which part of it were you able to accept as it was, and for what part did you require clarification?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I don't remember requiring any clarification for any of those reports. And I examined, I would say, most of the reports related to primary and secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would I then be right in saying that the main material you reviewed came from Mr. Baraybar, Mr. Lawrence, and who else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: When I was referring to these reports, I referred to all those experts which were, in a way, present during this exhumation process or later on, autopsy process. So there were many experts, like Bill Haglund, and you mentioned two. Then Richard Wright was present at some of those exhumations. So many of those experts, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't find there anything disputable or ambiguous that would require clarification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Nothing that would impact my conclusions in my report, in relation to these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And concerning numbers, was it your main task to establish the numbers or to update everything else that was done? Could you tell us specifically what was your assignment? To update what in Manning's work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I think I explained this morning what the objectives of my report were. There were four. They were not only to update numbers or to talk only about the numbers. That was only one objective, to update the numbers. The second one was to update the new located mass graves or graves or other locations which were related to Srebrenica events. Then the third one was to present the facts on surface remains. And the fourth one - and this is exclusively my one - was to analyse data to get DNA connections out of those data. And it was very important because those data, the DNA connections, actually corroborates what other experts have found before. So which mass graves are connected to the secondary grave-sites and -- et cetera. So it was additional corroboration of what they have been doing before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Now I understand. So you did not analyse that for accuracy. You were looking instead for elements to corroborate the findings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: No, both. I was critical to data which were already in our previous reports or in my -- my previous report. And I was critical to my own report when I excluded some of the -- the individuals which would appear, for example, in my Popovic report or even one site which is Srebrenica hospital. It's not here anymore. So I am always critical, and I am trying to find the facts. But you will always doing that because it's so many different locations and so many individuals on this list that certain mistakes may occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So some of the mistakes and omissions made by these experts, you were able to critically analyse, reconsider, and change the findings accordingly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. But these changes are really slight changes. It doesn't change anything significant in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in San Antonio, the work of institutions in charge of exhumations in Bosnia was reviewed critically and criticised, especially the work of Haglund/Kirschner? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I did hear about him being criticised - I'm referring to Dr. Haglund - but I'm not aware in detail about this criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that you, too, critically reviewed the material that you were supposed to update -- or, rather, to update the analyses of that initial work, don't you think it would have been useful to see what the San Antonio people found wrong with the work of Haglund/Kirschner and then decide what you think about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. And I think that this question is more for -- for Dr. Haglund, and I think he testified already in this case, and I'm sure you asked him this question as well. Because when -- what I was doing is putting all the evidence, all the documents on the records, and all the statements and whatever I was able to find to particular grave-site or grave, in order to put the puzzles together. So -- because if you are looking partially just into one report or into specific area of investigation, you would not get a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, although you collected all these elements, these elements are based on actions that the scientific group in San Antonio found a lot to criticise about. Why didn't you find out more about that criticism to see whether the material you received from these experts is reliable enough? Did you never wonder whether everything was impeccably done, indeed, before you got involved?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I simply don't have answer to this question, why I haven't consulted or tried to find this criticism. Perhaps I didn't think important because I did have other information, other evidence about certain crimes committed and perhaps I didn't feel much important or important enough to consult. But if you have this, we can discuss these documents, you can discuss. Because it's better always to be more specific because now we are talking about some general issues on what I've done, what I haven't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fine. If we have time left tomorrow, we'll see what we can do about this. But this leads me to the area of your relationship with the OTP. What relationship did you have with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I was investigator for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you subject to the Official Secrets Act? Were you able to have difference of opinions with the Prosecution, to confront them, to oppose them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: We are all, you know, subject to -- not to reveal any secrets, secret acts or anything, all working for the United Nations. We are all under this obligation. But for the second part of your question, if I was -- if I could have a different opinion with the Prosecution, yes, of course. I was not limited to -- to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But your main task was to provide support for the indictment; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yeah. In a way, yes. My task was to update the report, to present the new numbers, mass graves, graves, and other figures about the victims of the Srebrenica event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On several occasions today you mentioned that you were forced to deal with certain inclarities and confusions and for each of them, it seems, you found a rational explanation. That was page 70 where you spoke, in particular, about confusions in the Parsons's testimony on mass graves, and several other times you said there were inclarities but you have dealt with them. Did you deal with them as the Prosecution would have wished or as your professional standards dictate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Certainly as my professional standards dictate -- dictate me. There was no influence by the Prosecution, what I was given by the Prosecution, if you are talking now about this particular case. I was given the testimony of -- that part of the testimony of Dr. Parsons and asked to review his testimony and to see what I can find out. And I did find out certain discrepancies between his testimony and what are the facts what I found out during my investigation, and I revealed those to -- today. But there was no instruction by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 64 of today's transcript, you said something went wrong with the identification. That's also one of the confusions. Did you solve any of these confusions in favour of the Defence? Or, rather, in a way that could be useful to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You know, whenever there was a confusion or if I was not certain about the facts or certain about what I could see in the ICMP data, if there were discrepancies, I would always consult them myself or through my colleagues, in order to get clarification. This is -- one of such examples were the unique DNA profiles. Then I also consulted them in 2010 regarding the illogical DNA connections. I think we sent information to them about the errors we thought at the time would be -- would be in their data, so -- but it's up to them, again, to establish that and to correct them if there are errors. Also, as you can see, that now we have several -- we have four tabs in their data, and one tab is exclusively related to the excluded individuals as being related to the Srebrenica event. So they did take certain steps towards the verification of their data. And I would say that was prompted also by our requests in order to take a look into those data or some portions of those data more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the final outcome of that intervention of yours? Did they realise their mistake and correct it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. If they realised the mistake, they corrected the mistake or they provided us a reasonable explanation why this should appear there in certain way. So -- but most of them they corrected. But I have to emphasise these are really -- because it's a huge amount of data in their spreadsheet, we are here talking really about a small number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yesterday during our interview, you confirmed that you didn't know whether the ICMP had checked their findings against those of some other institutions or whether anyone else checked their findings independently in their laboratories. You said that some errors were found on their lists but the number of those errors was low. Would you then agree that the importance of those errors should have been left to the Trial Chamber to decide; whereas you should have only analysed them statistically, to establish their statistical import?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It is always, at the end of the day, the Trial Chamber's decision and -- about what certain evidence might -- might tell or what weight to certain evidence might be given. It's up to them. But it's up to me, of course, to present the facts. And I don't deny that I did find certain discrepancies in the ICMP data. I alerted about them. I sent additional clarifications to -- to the ICMP. They corrected them. But, again, I'm emphasising this is really small number of data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what would have happened, Mr. Janc, if you had not been so diligent and so perspicacious to find this? Would those errors remain uncorrected?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: This would be now really speculation because someone else might be dealing in a same manner as I was dealing. Maybe ICMP would identify those mistakes by themselves. I don't know what would happen. I don't have answer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what would have happened if you had been even more diligent and even more insightful and found out even more errors? In other words, could it be that there are more errors undetected?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. I think the witness called it himself, this just all requires speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the Defence teams of the people who have been already convicted on the basis of previous findings? Did you inform them of the latest you have established about all these errors?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I'm sure they are aware of those because I understand all of my reports are disclosed to any Defence team who might be interested in -- in it, or -- regardless of being already convicted or not. And if you follow these reports, you will see the differences which are, again, of course, small corrections, but, still, they are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were able to observe certain errors in the work of the ICMP, especially their lists. Does that mean that certain matters that could be ambiguous or undetermined in initial materials, such as the reports of Mr. Lawrence, Haglund, Baraybar, and Dean Manning, if there are any ambiguities there, or perhaps even errors, would they be perpetuated in Manning's reports and yours? Did you subject this initial material to additional analysis and verification?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I just say again that the majority of the ICMP data are valid, reliable and are not impacted by these errors. You are really talking about a small number of cases which might be ambiguous. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. My position is -- or, rather, the position of the Defence is that this significance can only be established by way of statistics, not just off the cuff; right? And you did not undertake the necessary statistical procedure.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I would say one of the ways is through statistics, but not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you claim that, on the basis of their findings, their initial findings that were analysed by Mr. Manning and then you inherited all of that and ultimately updated it, are you saying that you could have known when people fell victim, and can you link that to the period after Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes. They're linked to the period after Srebrenica. There are many evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I am asking you about the expert work of these people, these five people. What was it in their expertise that convinced you that these persons perished in the second week of July 1995? Are these autopsy results? What was it that could have confirmed that for you in order to be able to firmly assert that these victims were from the second week of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You know, we cannot partialise their work, let's put it this way. You have to have a complete picture. What I am getting from their reports, for example, pathologists, perhaps I'm not getting the date when certain individual was killed, executed or died, whatever. What I am getting is the manner of death and how it was found, where it was found, what kind of artefacts, evidence, or whatever, was found in the place where he was buried. So this is important what I am looking at. So in order to ascertain or, you know, to establish the dates, there are different means to doing that, and one of those - in this case it is very important - are the aerial images where you can see when those graves were opened, reopened and closed. Then, of course, we have so many evidence, documentary evidence, being statements, testimonies of those survived, of those witnesses of these killings or even participated in them. Then we have documents from the various sources, one of them being VRS, about the -- how they move the equipment around these places. So have you to take into consideration all of them, in order to get into a conclusion when certain individual might die. Those won't -- you, as an investigator, I know that you will never find or you will very rarely find information in -- in -- in such reports from these experts about the exact date or even time of death. Yes, if the body is fresh, then, yes. But if it is -- if some time elapsed, you won't find these conclusions there. But all sorts -- all other conclusions will be there which are important for investigation to ascertain or to find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today on page 6, line 16, that even from witnesses who took part in the killings, you obtained information. Did these witnesses disclose the names of their victims to you; and did you establish the time of death for these victims on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: There were several executors interviewed by the ICTY. Some of them, I think, testified also in this courtroom. Perhaps you are not provided with the names by those executors, but I think they described in detail who the people being killed by them were. We did get lots of names, on the other side, from the survivors, from the people being connected to those killed, walking through the woods. We have many, many of those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you confirmed that you proceed from an assumption that needs to be confirmed; namely, that all bodies found in mass graves belong to persons who were executed in the second week of July; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that. However, thanks to you, one of the corrections of ICMP findings was the fact that you established that in one mass grave, the mortal remains of some persons who lost their lives in 1993 were found; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I think you are now talking about Bljeceva 1, secondary grave, which is indeed a mixed grave. Being mixed, I mean inside, the individuals or victims of incident -- incident which happened in Bratunac, I think, in 1992, not 1993, were disposed also. In addition, some human remains from the victims of the Srebrenica events -- event were disposed into the same mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So at different points in time. Is it your position that that is the only grave in which people were buried at different points in time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You know, I don't claim here that people were buried in that location at different points in time. What I say, that they are coming from different events, the bodies which are disposed into this particular mass grave are coming from two different events. I would say - it's my opinion - they're coming at the same time but from two different locations. So both were buried somewhere else before, and they were reburied and disposed into this mass grave. And to answer your question, yes, I think this is the only mixed grave, mass grave, which I came across during this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you rule out the possibility of bodies or victims from 1992 being buried that point in time, and then the grave was opened again and victims from 1995 were added? How did you rule that out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Reviewing the exhumation records on that exhumation would tell us a lot. And I'm particularly referring to the ICMP summary report on that exhumation. Such discrepancies or such indications would be spotted during the exhumation itself. I think we have seven deposits inside that grave, and when they opened the grave, they spotted a difference between certain deposits. And, subsequently, I'm sure they would find out that -- or they would be spotted during their exhumation because I know that archeologists are also present during the exhumation and they would be able to say, yes, we have two sets of bodies inside this grave, actually bodies from different locations, and they were disposed into that grave in -- on two different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, they did not conclude that. You somehow came by that information; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. They haven't explicitly put down this conclusion in writing into their report. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you discover what the reason might have been for the reburial of victims from 1992, relocation into a new grave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: You know, it would be again speculation, whatever I say. But most probably the reason was the same as it was for the reburials which occurred in -- occurred in relation to Srebrenica event: To hide some crimes committed from someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh. Don't you think that 1992 was far away and that there was no reason for them to be brought out into broad daylight and reburied somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Nothing is too far away for the war crimes. And at that time I think there was already an investigation. It was well-known there would be or the investigation is ongoing against the high-level officials in Bratunac. And perhaps that was the reason. I'm now specific referring to Mr. Deronjic, Miroslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do I understand this correctly: Are you saying that the persons who were carrying out the exhumations, as well as the pathologists, could ascertain different times of death or different times of burial, in accordance with the corpses themselves, the existence of groups, and so on? What was it that they actually concluded?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I think we discussed the issue about the time of death. That one is difficult to establish just reviewing the -- the autopsy or -- for the pathologists. In relation to how the grave is created, I'm sure the archaeologists at the site would be able to ascertain. And they were, for example, able to ascertain how many deposits is there which simply means how many trucks came and dump bodies into the grave. And they ascertained also that soil found inside the grave is connected to the one from the primary site, and they concluded, based on that -- or it can be concluded based on that that there is only -- there are only bodies from one location deposited there at one point in time, also in connection with other evidence, other evidence we have available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what was the conclusion? From where were these bodies brought in, those that belonged to victims of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Now we are focussing on 1992. I have to admit, I haven't investigated that part of the incident. So I have no knowledge about where they are coming from. I do know there was some killing in 1992 in Bratunac, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So would you agree with Dr. Lawrence in the following: That the time of death or the time of burial, and very often not even the cause of death, cannot be established in many cases when bodies are so highly decomposed? I can even give you the page references for when he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it. The time of death and the time of burial cannot be established in that way. This is what he said on page 22483, lines 9 through 11. And the time of death cannot be established. He said that a pathologist could not do that. And he said that on page 22484, line 7 to 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of what did you establish that these were victims from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: First, yes, I agree with Dr. Lawrence. If you are reviewing or examining these records partially without having a picture about everything what happened and about the other evidence, that might be conclusion, yes. We cannot say when they were executed, when they were put in these graves. In that sense, I can agree with him. But you -- just let me confirm ... Ah-ha. You know, it's -- people which are in these graves appear on the ICRC missing list, so it means they went missing after the fall of Srebrenica. This is our basic source for information about the people found in these graves. In corroboration with other evidence, you will find even more information about these people. For example, when they went missing, when they were last seen by someone. You would have so many witnesses and victims of this crime -- crimes, giving us statements or testifying in court and naming those people who appeared in these graves. We do have aerial images. We have document evidence as to when they were excavated or when the machinery was employed into these locations. So when you put all this together, yes, we can conclude when they were actually executed, and when they were buried, and when they were reburied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How are you going to conclude that they were executed? On the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Okay. For that, we'll have to take a look into evidence, into what was found during exhumation. For example, that's where I would be looking first. And in many of those graves, there were many, many of shell casings around the area where they were buried as well. Then you have bullets inside the graves. You have then testimonies of people saying they were killed. Then have you in many of those graves, people were blindfolded and ligatured. Then you have evidence statement or a conclusion of the pathologist, I think, also that they were executed or that they were even alive buried and this kind -- these sorts of things. So these are all the evidence and all the main points I would be looking at when concluding when -- and actually what happened to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, or did you establish the number of victims who had ligatures on both hands? Real ligatures. Not bands or something like that, but real ligatures.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I do have a number of how many ligatures and blindfolds were found in these graves, the total number. If you allow, I can consult my spreadsheet and I will give you the numbers. Again, approximate numbers, because for some of them we can really -- we were unable to say, Okay, is this ligature or not. But I can give you, for example, the list or the numbers, how many of those were found in graves, if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, this is the not the first time you appear before the court; right? So do tell us what the number of indubitable ligatures is, beyond any doubt whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Okay. In order to do -- to give you the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tomorrow will be fine. Tomorrow will do. You will have a free evening, and you can take a look at all of that. We are here to establish what the truth is, not to claim victory. On the basis of the findings of pathologists, did you manage to conclude that someone had been executed; and, if so, what from distance, what kinds of ammunition was used? Do you have hard evidence? Was any of that established beyond any doubt? And on the basis of whose findings did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: I think there are many autopsy reports saying that -- that there are so many wounds, injuries, inside certain bodies, or the pathologist was certain that these people should be executed. In relation to the distance, I don't think I have ever seen any such conclusion or any such evidence on it, but there might be. In relation to what kind of ammunition was used, I think it's been established, because there are so many bullets found, shell casings found, and mainly it was -- it was the ammunition used at the time by the VRS army. And just to comment in relation to the ligatures, I'm not sure I would be able to do this analysis tonight. I have the numbers here. The problem is that these numbers won't be what you would like to have from me. In order to do that, I would need more time and access to the actual database which I don't have here, but I can provide you with -- with -- with the data, how many of those ligatures were found straight away. For example, for Branjevo and related Cancari graves, we have 274 -- sorry, 276. For Kozluk site and related Cancari graves, we have 313 ligatures. Then we go down. For Petkovci and related Liplje secondary graves, we have 72 ligatures. And for Orahovac and related Hodzici graves, we only have six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: And I also have numbers for blindfolds, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll deal that if we have enough time. That is even more controversial. However, Mr. Janc, the information I have is that there were 430 with ligatures, whereas some bands or ribbons on one hand can be disputed. 430, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you know Mr. Janc is not the proper witness to deal with that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take into account the fact that you mentioned a moment ago, that in the graves shell casings were found? And do you remember that in one grave each large calibre casings were found? I think that was Nova Kasaba or somewhere. Did you come across that information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did see that one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which situation, Mr. Janc, do casings fall into a grave, especially those coming from large calibres? Does that happen if the fire -- the fire is coming into that grave, or, if one fires from that grave, or, rather, trench? Where do -- where can casings be found? Where do they fall? Where the target is, or where the firing is actually taking place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC
utterances.text: It can be actually anywhere. Anywhere you can find the shell casings. Whenever -- you know, if you are firing, it would be usually behind you somewhere. If you are inside a trench, it may be found outside or inside the trench. And usually they are -- they are behind or, you know, to one of your sides. That's how usually the ammunition works.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, is it time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's about time to adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.59 p.m.,
